claim: Virendra Kumar (2020) treats Rule 180 compliance as obligatory, held that a CoI-stage Rule 180 lapse not raised at charge, Summary of Evidence or trial could not ground a post-trial remand for a fresh CoI, and limited AFT retrial/remand power.
original_text: The Supreme Court distinguished obligatory Rule 180 opportunity from the consequence of procedural defects at an earlier fact-finding stage. It held that in the facts of the case a CoI lapse raised only after full trial did not warrant a remand to conduct a fresh CoI, and discussed limits on AFT retrial/remand authority.
rationale: Official PDF read. Para 12(b) and (d): accused entitled to full opportunity under Rule 180 and authorities must rectify if the ground is raised at charge or Summary of Evidence stage because compliance 'is obligatory'. Para 13: non-compliance existed but was not raised at charge, summary of evidence or court-martial; after full trial not open to raise it; Tribunal ought not to have remanded for de novo inquiry from CoI stage. Para 15: AFT may order retrial only on s.16(2) AFT Act grounds; non-compliance of Rule 180 cannot ground retrial; no power to remand to a stage prior to court-martial. The record's summary is supported. Note para 12(c) states more broadly that irregularities at earlier stages cannot be the basis for setting aside the court-martial order (a distillation of earlier case law); the record's 'in the facts' framing is the narrower and safer reading. The Court remanded the Transfer Application to the AFT for decision on merits (para 15) - not mentioned in the record.
advisor_questions: Should the record state that the SC remanded the Transfer Application to the AFT for merits, so readers do not treat Virendra Kumar as a final validation of the court-martial?
Does para 12(c) (earlier-stage irregularities cannot set aside a court-martial) carry precedential weight given the judgment is marked Non-Reportable?

claim: The BSA 2023 applies to judicial proceedings including courts-martial; admissibility of electronic records and certificates depend on current provisions and facts.
original_text: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam applies to judicial proceedings including courts-martial. Digital evidence can be important, but admissibility, authenticity, lawful acquisition and certificates depend on exact current provisions and facts.
rationale: BSA s.1(2) (India Code): 'It applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court, including Courts-martial'. BSA s.61-62 make electronic records provable under s.63, and s.63(4) requires a certificate submitted with the electronic record 'at each instance where it is being submitted for admission'. Under the former Evidence Act, Anvar P.V. (paras 13-15, 22) held a s.65B(4) certificate a condition of admissibility of secondary electronic evidence, and Arjun Panditrao (para 72(b)) clarified that no certificate is needed where the original device is itself produced. The record's caution that certificates depend on exact provisions and facts, and its emphasis on preserving originals rather than screenshots, is consistent with these authorities.
advisor_questions: Do Anvar/Arjun carry over to BSA s.63 for proceedings after 1 July 2024? No post-BSA SC authority was checked.
limitations: No judgment interpreting BSA s.63 was located or read.
Lawful acquisition / device-search limb not checked.

claim: AFT Act s.14 governs service-matter applications; s.15 gives appellate jurisdiction over court-martial orders, decisions, findings or sentences, with powers on conviction, sentence, bail and enhancement after hearing.
original_text: Section 14 governs service-matter applications. Section 15 provides appellate jurisdiction over an order, decision, finding or sentence passed by court-martial, with specified powers over conviction, sentence and bail.
rationale: AFT Act (India Code): s.14(1)-(2) service matters and applications; s.15(1)-(2) appeal against 'any order, decision, finding or sentence passed by a court-martial'; s.15(3) bail; s.15(4)-(5) allowing appeals against conviction; s.15(6)(a)-(f) substitution, remission/mitigation/commutation, and (c) enhancement with proviso 'no such sentence shall be enhanced unless the appellant has been given an opportunity of being heard'. The record's statements and its 'power to enhance after hearing' risk line match the text. Parashotam Dass (para 11, a private-party submission) notes HCs' reluctance to entertain writs against s.15 orders - not a holding.

No AFT or SC judgment on the s.14/s.15 boundary was read.

claim: The example of a soldier dismissed by SCM needs s.3(o) analysis: 'service matters' expressly include trials where dismissal is awarded and SCMs with dismissal or >3 months' imprisonment, so the s.14/s.15 routes can overlap; the record's 'do not force a trial appeal into a generic service-law cause of action' is not anchored to any judgment.
original_text: Example: A soldier dismissed by a SCM must receive a distinct jurisdiction analysis under ss3(o),14 and 15.
rationale: AFT Act s.3(o)(iii) includes 'summary disposal and trials where the punishment of dismissal is awarded' and the exclusion in item (iv) carves back SCMs 'where the punishment is of dismissal or imprisonment for more than three months'. An SCM is a court-martial for s.15 purposes. The statute therefore places such a dismissal within both 'service matters' and s.15 appeal. The record's example correctly flags the need for analysis, but the preceding risk statement could be read as excluding a s.14 application; no judicial authority on the choice of route was located in this pass.
advisor_questions: Is there controlling AFT/SC authority on whether a SCM dismissal is challenged by s.14 OA, s.15 appeal, or either?

claim: Anvar was reaffirmed with clarification by Arjun Panditrao (2020) para 72(b); for current proceedings BSA ss.61-63 apply.
original_text: Arjun (2020) para 72(b) reaffirms Anvar (2014), with clarification on original device evidence.
rationale: Arjun para 72(a): 'Anvar P.V. (supra), as clarified by us hereinabove, is the law declared by this Court on Section 65B'; Tomaso Bruno and Shafhi Mohammad overruled. Para 72(b): certificate unnecessary if the original document itself is produced (owner proving the device); where the computer is part of a system/network that cannot be brought to court, s.65B(1) with a s.65B(4) certificate is the only route; Anvar para 24's words 'under Section 62 of the Evidence Act' are to be read out. The row's treatment status and scope caveat (BSA ss.61-63 for current proceedings) are consistent with BSA ss.61-63 as enacted.
limitations: Concurring opinion in Arjun not reviewed.
